newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: IMF loan to Pakistan clouded by Bhutto ouster.
newsitem.headline: IMF loan to Pakistan clouded by Bhutto ouster.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is continuing talks with Pakistan over a stalled $600 million standby loan, but the government's ouster has cast uncertainty over the deal, banking officials said on Tuesday.
The bankers, who asked not to be identified, said a visiting IMF team briefly met Pakistani civil servants on Tuesday.

President Farooq Leghari sacked Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto early on Tuesday, accusing her government of corruption. He named former parliament speaker Meraj Khalid, 80, as interim prime minister pending general elections set for February 3.

Pakistani and IMF officials expect to endorse technical changes to a draft letter of intent on Wednesday. It would then have to be cleared by the caretaker government and IMF management before an IMF decision on whether to release delayed tranches of the loan.
"They (the IMF) are going ahead on this," one banker said. "They are completing the work they were supposed to do."

IMF director Paul Chabrier had been due to arrive in Islamabad from Saudi Arabia on Tuesday to try to complete the agreement. But his flight from Riyadh was cancelled, and he decided to scrap his visit as he had to be back in Washington by the week's end, an IMF official said.
The banking officials said there was a widespread expectation that the caretaker government would adhere to the same general economic policies as Bhutto's three-year government.
"There are indications that the economic policy will stay the course," one banker said.
But the IMF would need to be sure that policy commitments spelled out in the letter of intent would extend beyond the proposed three-month life of the interim government, he said.

"Some actions go beyond the three-month period," one official said. "There needs to be some kind of assurance that it will go ahead beyond three months. But it is not clear what assurance would be acceptable to the IMF."
The fate of the standby loan would also depend on the reaction of financial markets to the change of government.
"If there is capital flight due to uncertainty, some of the projections would change," a banker said.
The rupee closed 0.10 rupee up at 42.98 to the dollar on Tuesday in the kerb market as players sold dollars to invest in stocks after Bhutto's government was sacked, dealers said.
They said the rupee was likely to rise further on Wednesday as more investors switch out of the dollar to join what brokers said would be a bull-run on the Karachi bourse.
The stock exchange was closed for a scheduled holiday on Tuesday, but investors did brisk kerb trade in its parking lot, with favoured scrips posting substantial gains, dealers said.
Money rates were relatively unaffected by Leghari's dismissal of Benazir's three-year-old government.

Asked if the caretaker government would endorse the letter of intent, a banker said: "One cannot be sure of that. If the government says it is OK and the markets are calm, we can go ahead. There's some uncertainty. We just have to wait and see."

Last month, Bhutto's government devalued the rupee, imposed new taxes, cut spending and raised fuel prices by 10 percent under an emergency package designed to stave off a possible foreign exchange crisis and regain IMF favour.
